title: Unit – 2 : Session – 5 : SLO – 1 | Memory Locations and Addresses
sections: Section A – Match the Following (Answers)
1. Word Length → D. Number of bits grouped and accessed together
2. Byte → C. A group of 8 bits
3. Main Memory → A. Collection of storage locations with unique identifiers
4. Address → E. Unique identifier for a word in memory
5. Address Space → B. Minimum number of bits needed to represent all memory locations
Section B – Fill in the Blanks
The term BYTE refers to a group of 8 bits.
A word of 16 bits is commonly referred to as a HALF word.
The total number of uniquely identifiable locations in memory is called the ADDRESS SPACE.
Each storage location in memory has a unique identifier called an ADDRESS.
To access 32 MB of memory byte-wise, we need 25 bits for addressing (32 MB = 2^25 bytes).
Section C – Activity Task
Task 1a: 64 MB memory, word = 4 bytes → number of words = 64M/4 = 16M = 2^24 → 24 bits are needed to address a word.
Task 1b: 1 GB memory, word = 8 bytes → number of words = 2^30 / 2^3 = 2^27 → 27 bits are required to address each word.

Task 2 – Memory layout (described): a column of words from address 0 (first word) to 2^k – 1 (last word); each row is one n-bit word; the i-th word sits at address i; addresses label the rows, the n-bit contents are the data.
Section D – True or False
A byte is made up of 16 bits. — FALSE (8 bits)
Memory addresses are expressed using unsigned binary numbers. — TRUE
The main memory stores data in single bits only. — FALSE
The term 'address space' refers to the number of address lines available. — FALSE
In computer hardware, names are used to identify memory locations. — FALSE (binary addresses are used)
